title: A Song for God's City
overview: This psalm celebrates Jerusalem, especially Mount Zion where the temple stood, as safe because God is present there, recalling a time when enemy kings turned back in fear.

parts.label: God makes the city great (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The song praises God first and the city second, because Zion's beauty and safety come from God being present among its people. The poem links Zion with the lofty north, and Zaphon, a famous northern mountain, was treated in neighboring peoples' stories as the home of the gods, so the poem is likely saying Zion is the true mountain of God.

parts.label: Enemy kings turn and run (vv. 4-7)
parts.note: Allied kings march on the city, but one look at it fills them with panic and they flee, shaking like a woman in labor. Scholars are unsure which event is meant, perhaps an alliance defeated in King Jehoshaphat's day or the Assyrian retreat in 701 BC, and the ships of Tarshish, the largest trading ships, wrecked by a fierce east wind, picture how suddenly great power can be broken.

parts.label: Seen with our own eyes (v. 8)
parts.note: The people had heard old stories of God protecting the city, and now they say they have watched it happen themselves. From that they draw the hope that God will keep the city secure for good.

parts.label: Worship in the temple (vv. 9-11)
parts.note: Gathered at the temple, the people reflect on God's faithful love and expect praise for God to spread as far as God's reputation. Zion and the smaller towns of Judah around it are glad because God has acted fairly and decisively.

parts.label: Walk around and tell it (vv. 12-14)
parts.note: Worshipers are invited to circle the city, count its towers and study its walls so they can describe it to their children as living proof of God's care. The Hebrew of the last line is unclear: translations say God guides to the end or even to death, and some scholars think the closing words may be a musical note that drifted in.

disagreement: Since Jerusalem was later destroyed, Christians differ on whether the promise that God will make the city secure forever points mainly to the earthly Jerusalem, to the church as God's people, or to a future heavenly city.
think: If you could walk the next generation around one place or story to show them what you have found trustworthy, what would you choose, and why that one?
